subject: Science
theme: Supercomputing milestone—performance measurement units and the teraflop barrier
question_short_text: World's fastest computer performance capability in December 1996
text: The world's fastest computer has been able to perform (as of Dec. 1996):
explanation: As of December 1996, ASCI Red became the first supercomputer to break the teraflop barrier, achieving approximately 1 trillion (10¹²) floating-point operations per second.

research.summary: The teraflop milestone in December 1996 marks a watershed moment in computing history. ASCI Red (Accelerated Strategic Computing Initiative—Option Red), built by Intel and installed at Sandia National Laboratories, became the world's first computer to exceed 1 trillion floating-point operations per second (FLOPS), measured on the MP-LINPACK benchmark. The measurement matters: 10⁶ = megaflop, 10⁹ = gigaflop, 10¹² = teraflop, 10¹⁵ = petaflop. In December 1996, three-quarters of the system achieved 1.06 TFLOPS sustained performance, eventually reaching 2.38 TFLOPS after processor upgrades. This was a decisive leap beyond the Hitachi SR2201 (600 gigaflops in 1996) and decades ahead of contemporary scientific expectations. The trap for students is conflating FLOPS with simple arithmetic operations—these are specifically floating-point operations, crucial for scientific and weapons simulation. ASCI Red was built for the U.S. Department of Energy's nuclear weapons stewardship program following the 1992 nuclear testing moratorium; it needed to perform complex 3D simulations using commodity Pentium Pro processors (9,298 of them) connected via mesh topology, not exotic vector chips. The machine dominated the TOP500 rankings from June 1997 to June 2000 and earned legendary status for reliability.
facts: A teraflop = 1 trillion floating-point operations per second; by 2024, exascale supercomputers exceed 1.1 × 10¹⁸ FLOPS (1.1 exaflops), a billion-fold increase in 28 years

ASCI Red used 9,298 off-the-shelf Intel Pentium Pro processors running at 200 MHz (later upgraded to 333 MHz Pentium II), proving massively parallel commodity processors could beat specialized vector architectures
ASCI Red held the world's fastest supercomputer title for nearly four years (June 1997 to late 2000), the longest reign of any top-ranked machine in modern supercomputing history
The LINPACK benchmark, not peak theoretical FLOPS, defines official rankings; ASCI Red's sustained 1.06 TFLOPS was measured on MP-LINPACK, the distributed-memory variant
Prior to ASCI Red, the Japanese Hitachi SR2201 (November 1996) held the top spot with 368.2 GFLOPS—nearly 3 times slower than ASCI Red's teraflop achievement
